questions.title: What is Claude Code, and how would a lead evaluate and introduce it?
questions.quick: As I understand it, Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool that works in the terminal and IDE integrations: it reads the repository, edits files, runs commands and iterates against tests. I would pilot it on real tickets, compare defect and rework data, use a shared CLAUDE.md for conventions, keep permissions tight, and require normal pull requests and CI. Because features change often, I would verify current documentation and enterprise controls before committing.
questions.revision: Agentic terminal coding tool: pilot on real tickets, shared instruction file, tight permissions, normal PR and CI gates, verify current docs.
questions.detailed:
**Claude Code** is, to my understanding, Anthropic's agentic coding assistant. It runs in a terminal (with editor integrations) and can read a codebase, propose and make edits, run shell commands and tests, and loop on the results. It differs from autocomplete because it acts on the repository, not just the cursor position.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

A developer describes a task, the agent explores relevant files, proposes a plan, edits, runs the test suite and linter, and reports. Humans approve actions through a permission model and then commit through the normal branch and PR process. A project instruction file (CLAUDE.md) carries build commands and conventions.

## Good use cases

Bounded changes with clear tests: bug fixes, test writing, mechanical refactors, codebase questions, scripting, documentation drafts, and migrations split into reviewable steps.

## Limitations and risks

It can produce plausible but wrong code, drift from conventions when context is thin, and make large unreviewable diffs. Because it can run commands, a loose permission setting widens the blast radius. Cost and usage limits matter for heavy agentic use.

## Git and CI integration

Work on a branch, small commits, standard PR review. CI remains the gate: tests, linting, static analysis, dependency and secret scanning. Some teams run the CLI headlessly in CI for review or triage; treat that as a separate, scoped-token decision.

## Security implications

Prompt injection through files or issues is the main concern, plus secrets in the working directory and data leaving the machine. Use least-privilege permissions, deny lists for sensitive paths, no production credentials, and confirm the vendor's data-retention and enterprise terms.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Run a time-boxed pilot with a control group. Track lead time, review effort, change failure rate, escaped defects and rework within 30 days, plus developer feedback. Do not count lines or prompts.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Start with a volunteer cohort, approved repositories and a written usage standard. Configure managed settings and permission defaults centrally if supported, agree on review rules for AI-assisted changes, involve security and legal early, and publish what is and is not allowed.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How would you restrict what the agent can run?
What goes in a CLAUDE.md and what does not?
How would you compare it with an IDE-based assistant?

questions.title: What is Cursor, and how would a lead assess it for a team?
questions.quick: As I understand it, Cursor is an AI-first code editor built on the VS Code lineage, combining inline completion, chat over the codebase, and an agent mode that edits multiple files. I would assess it on our repositories for review effort and defect rates, manage project rules files, check privacy and data-handling modes, and keep CI and PR review unchanged. I would verify current features, pricing and enterprise controls first.
questions.revision: AI-first VS Code-style editor with chat, completion and agent mode: assess on real repos, manage rules, check privacy modes, keep CI gates.
questions.detailed:
**Cursor** is, as I understand it, an AI-focused code editor derived from the VS Code ecosystem. It offers inline completion, codebase-aware chat, and an agent mode that can plan and edit across files. It is an IDE replacement rather than a plug-in, which matters for rollout.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Developers open a project, index the codebase, ask questions or request changes in chat or agent mode, review diffs inline, accept or reject hunks, and run tests in the integrated terminal. Project rules files carry conventions into prompts.

## Good use cases

Interactive work where a developer wants to stay in the editor: feature work in familiar code, exploratory refactors, test generation, and learning an unfamiliar module with codebase questions.

## Limitations and risks

Being a separate editor means extension, settings and security reviews are needed. Agent edits across many files can be hard to review. Quality depends on context selection, and developers may over-trust accepted diffs.

## Git and CI integration

The editor works on a normal Git checkout, so branching, PRs and CI are unchanged. Keep generated changes small and let CI be the gate. Rules files can be committed so the team shares conventions.

## Security implications

Check what code and prompts are sent to which providers, whether a privacy or no-retention mode exists, how codebase indexing is stored, and which extensions are permitted. Handle secrets files with ignore settings and never rely on the editor alone.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Compare against a baseline on the same ticket types: review time, rework, defect escapes, and developer-reported friction. Run it side by side with another tool in a spike, not by opinion.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Approve it through the normal software-approval route, define allowed models and modes, pin configuration, publish a rules baseline, and train on review discipline. Offer it as one sanctioned option rather than a mandate.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How do you decide between an AI editor and a terminal agent?
How would you stop sensitive files being indexed?
What would make you reject it after a pilot?

questions.title: What is Windsurf, and how would you evaluate it for enterprise use?
questions.quick: My understanding is that Windsurf is an AI-native IDE with an agentic assistant called Cascade, aimed at working across a codebase with awareness of what the developer is doing. Because ownership and product direction in this market have shifted, I would verify its current status, roadmap and enterprise terms before any pilot. Evaluation criteria and governance would match any other assistant: real repositories, measured outcomes, standard PR and CI gates.
questions.revision: AI-native IDE with an agentic assistant: verify current ownership, roadmap and enterprise terms, then evaluate like any assistant.
questions.detailed:
**Windsurf** is, to my understanding, an AI-native IDE (originally associated with Codeium) featuring an agentic assistant named Cascade. I am less certain of its current ownership and roadmap, since this market has seen acquisitions and licensing changes. Treat vendor continuity as a real evaluation criterion and confirm it from current sources.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

A developer works in the IDE, asks the agent to carry out a multi-step task, reviews proposed edits, runs commands with approval and iterates. Rules or memory features may carry conventions across sessions; verify what is currently supported.

## Good use cases

Similar to other agentic editors: feature slices, refactors, test generation, and exploring unfamiliar code where in-editor flow helps.

## Limitations and risks

Vendor and roadmap uncertainty, the same multi-file review burden as other agents, and variation in model choice and quality. Lock-in to editor-specific rules or memory formats is a hidden cost.

## Git and CI integration

Uses a normal Git working copy, so PRs and CI stay the gate. Keep conventions in portable files (for example AGENTS.md) where tools allow, so switching tools is cheap.

## Security implications

Review data handling, retention, self-hosting or zero-retention options, command-execution approvals, and extension policy. Seek security attestations the vendor publishes and verify them rather than assume.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Run the same ticket set through each candidate, comparing review effort, defects, rework and developer experience. Include vendor risk and exit cost in the scorecard.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Include procurement and security review, set permission defaults, keep rules portable, and define an exit plan. Pilot with a small group and re-evaluate quarterly because the product may change materially.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How do you reduce tool lock-in?
What vendor-risk questions would you ask?
How would you compare it fairly with Cursor?

questions.title: What is Amp, and how would you decide whether it belongs in your toolset?
questions.quick: As I understand it, Amp is a coding agent from the Sourcegraph lineage, available as a CLI and editor extension, built around agentic workflows and shareable threads. I am not certain of its current packaging or its exact corporate relationship, so I would verify current documentation. I would evaluate it like other agents: scoped pilot, permissions, review discipline, measured outcomes and security review.
questions.revision: Agentic coding tool from the Sourcegraph lineage with CLI and threads: verify packaging, pilot, scope permissions, measure outcomes.
questions.detailed:
**Amp** most plausibly refers to the coding agent associated with Sourcegraph. My understanding is that it is an agentic tool used from a CLI or editor, with threads that can be shared and a focus on multi-model, tool-using workflows. The official manual describes it as a coding agent and development environment; I could not confirm details such as the current Sourcegraph relationship from that page, so treat that as uncertain.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

A developer gives the agent a task, it explores code (Sourcegraph's heritage is code search), edits, runs commands and reports in a thread. Threads can be saved or shared for review, and an AGENTS.md file may carry instructions.

## Good use cases

Cross-repository understanding, larger refactors needing good search, and sharing agent sessions for teaching or review. Whether it suits a given team depends on current features.

## Limitations and risks

Younger tool with changing pricing and features; threads may contain code and decisions that need retention rules; same risks of unreviewable diffs and over-trust.

## Git and CI integration

Run it on a branch, review via normal PRs, and keep CI as the gate. Where agents run in remote environments, check how repository access and tokens are granted.

## Security implications

Examine where code and thread content are stored, who can view shared threads, how credentials reach remote environments, and tool-execution approvals. Use scoped, short-lived tokens.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Measure the same outcomes as other tools. The unique question is whether shared threads improve review and learning enough to justify any extra process.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Treat as an optional sanctioned tool after security review; define a sharing policy for threads, use portable instruction files, and review costs after a pilot.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: What would you check about shared thread data?
When does code search matter for an agent?
How would you present this to a security team?

questions.title: How do GitHub Copilot agent mode and the Copilot coding agent differ, and how would you govern them?
questions.quick: My understanding is that agent mode works in the editor, where a developer watches and steers multi-file edits and terminal steps. The coding agent is asynchronous: you assign an issue, it works in a GitHub-hosted environment and opens a pull request for review. Governance centres on repository permissions, branch protection, required reviews and CI. I would verify current plan, policy and feature details in GitHub's documentation.
questions.revision: Agent mode is interactive in the editor; coding agent works asynchronously from an issue and opens a PR. Govern with branch protection, reviews and CI.
questions.detailed:
As I understand it, **GitHub Copilot** now spans several modes: completion, chat, **agent mode** in the IDE (interactive multi-step editing and terminal use), and the **coding agent**, which takes an assigned issue, works in an isolated GitHub-hosted environment and raises a pull request. Names and availability change, so verify them against current GitHub documentation.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Interactive: describe a task, approve steps, review diffs. Asynchronous: write a well-specified issue, assign it, wait for a draft PR, then review and comment to iterate. Copilot can honour repository instruction files.

## Good use cases

The asynchronous mode suits well-specified, low-risk tickets: small bugs, tests, documentation, dependency or lint clean-up. Interactive mode suits exploratory feature work.

## Limitations and risks

Vague issues produce vague PRs. Large generated diffs raise review load. Agent-authored PRs may need workflow approval before CI runs, and the tool does not replace design judgement.

## Git and CI integration

This is its native strength: work happens in branches and PRs, with Actions as the gate. Use branch protection, required reviewers and status checks so the agent cannot merge itself.

## Security implications

The agent acts with repository access, so apply least privilege, restrict network access where configurable, treat issue text as untrusted input (prompt injection) and keep secrets out of its environment. Confirm organisation-level policy controls.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Compare agent-PR merge rate, review iterations, escaped defects and time to merge against human PRs of the same type. A high merge rate with high rework is not success.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Enable by policy for selected repositories, require human approval on every agent PR, document which ticket types are eligible, and review audit logs. Keep issue templates strict to improve spec quality.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How do you stop an agent PR merging itself?
What makes an issue suitable for assignment?
How would you handle a malicious issue description?

questions.title: What is the BMAD method in practice, and what are its strengths and limits?
questions.quick: The BMad Method is an open-source framework for agile AI-driven development. It provides role-based agents for product, architecture, UX, development and testing, and keeps briefs, specifications and architecture documents as explicit artefacts that carry context between sessions. It scales from small changes to larger planning. I would trial it on one project, adapt it, and verify the current version, which has had notable changes.
questions.revision: Open-source agile AI-development framework with role agents and persistent artefacts: trial, adapt, verify current version.
questions.detailed:
**BMad Method** (the repository calls it the Breakthrough Method for Agile AI-Driven Development) is an open-source framework that installs agents and workflows into your AI tool. Its README describes specialised agents for product, architecture, UX, development and testing, explicit planning artefacts such as briefs, specifications and architecture documents, and a learn-and-adjust loop. It reports a stable v6 line and a changing V7 preview, so details move.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Install into a project, then brief the idea, write a specification, define architecture, split work into stories, implement and test story by story, and feed learning back into the plan. Small changes can skip heavy planning.

## Good use cases

Greenfield or sizeable features where planning artefacts reduce re-explaining, and teams that benefit from consistent roles and handoffs.

## Limitations and risks

Ceremony can outweigh value on small work. Generated documents can look authoritative while being wrong. The framework changes between versions and depends on Node, Python and tooling versions.

## Git and CI integration

Artefacts are Markdown files in the repository, so they are versioned and reviewable in PRs. CI does not need to know about the method, but you can add checks for stale or missing specs.

## Security implications

Install scripts and agent definitions are code you run: pin versions, review what is installed and treat third-party prompts as supply-chain items. Documents may capture sensitive design detail, so apply repository access rules.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Compare ticket-to-merge time, rework due to misunderstood requirements, and defects against a control. Also ask whether specs were kept current.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Pilot on one non-critical project, adapt the roles to your own SDLC rather than adopting everything, pin the version and name an owner. Keep human approval at each artefact gate.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How would you stop specs going stale?
When would you skip the method?
How do you review an AI-written architecture document?

questions.title: What is Gas Town, and should an enterprise use multi-agent orchestrators like it?
questions.quick: As I understand it, Gas Town is Steve Yegge's open-source workspace manager for coordinating many AI coding agents. Its README describes a Mayor coordinator, rigs wrapping repositories, worker agents called polecats, monitoring roles and a merge-queue Refinery, with work state stored in git-backed hooks. It looks experimental and cost-intensive, so I would study it, not deploy it for production work without a tightly sandboxed pilot.
questions.revision: Open-source orchestrator for many coding agents (Mayor, rigs, polecats, Refinery): study and sandbox-pilot, not production-first.
questions.detailed:
**Gas Town** is an open-source multi-agent workspace manager by Steve Yegge. The README describes a **Mayor** as coordinator, **rigs** wrapping git repositories, **polecats** as worker agents with persistent identity but ephemeral sessions, a **Witness** and **Deacon** for health and supervision, and a **Refinery** merge queue. Work items are beads grouped into convoys. It supports several agent CLIs. The README does not clearly state a maturity level, so I would treat it as early and fast-moving.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Tell the Mayor what to build, it creates and groups beads, assigns them to agents, agents persist state in hooks, and finished work flows through the merge queue.

## Good use cases

Research into parallel agent workflows, large decomposable backlogs, and learning what coordination problems appear at scale.

## Limitations and risks

Many parallel agents amplify cost, review load and merge conflicts. Failure modes multiply, and some presets run in autonomous modes. Accountability for each change is harder to trace.

## Git and CI integration

Its Refinery batches work, runs checks and merges, so CI and merge rules must be configured to be the real gate. Never let it bypass branch protection or required review.

## Security implications

Autonomous modes with broad tool trust are risky. Run in disposable sandboxes with no production credentials, restrict network and token scope, and treat dashboards as local-trusted surfaces.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Measure merged-and-kept changes, defect escapes, review hours and cost per accepted change, not agent count or activity.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Keep it in a research lane: isolated environment, non-critical repository, explicit budget, human review before merge, and a written conclusion at the end of the spike.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: What does parallel agent work do to review load?
How do you attribute a change to an agent?
What sandbox would you require?

questions.title: What is Beads, and why might agents need their own issue tracker?
questions.quick: Beads, or bd, is Steve Yegge's tracker for AI coding agents. The README describes a dependency-aware graph of tasks with hash-based IDs, JSON output, a ready command for unblocked work and compaction of old tasks. It stores data in Dolt, synced through a git remote. The idea is persistent, structured memory instead of loose markdown plans. I would pilot it for long-running agent work and verify the current storage details.
questions.revision: Dependency-graph issue tracker for agents on Dolt: persistent structured memory, ready-work queries; pilot and verify storage details.
questions.detailed:
**Beads** (`bd`) is described in its README as a distributed graph issue tracker for AI coding agents, built on Dolt. Tasks (beads) form a dependency graph with hash-based IDs to avoid merge collisions, and agents can ask for work with no open blockers. Earlier versions were described differently (JSONL-based), so verify what the current release does.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Create a bead, link dependencies, run `bd ready` to find unblocked work, claim it atomically, work and close it, which releases dependants. `bd prime` gives an agent its context.

## Good use cases

Long agent tasks where plans exceed a context window, multiple agents needing shared state, and discovering follow-up work mid-task.

## Limitations and risks

Another tool and data store to learn and secure. Agents may create noisy or duplicate beads. Human stakeholders still need to see work in the team's real tracker.

## Git and CI integration

State syncs through a git remote, so access control follows the repository. CI does not need it, but a reconciliation step linking beads to PRs and the main tracker avoids drift.

## Security implications

Task text can carry sensitive detail and can be an injection vector if agents read untrusted beads. Control who can write, and treat bead content as untrusted input.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Compare completed-task accuracy, rework, and the time humans spend reconstructing state, with and without it.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Use alongside, not instead of, the official tracker; pilot with a small team, define ownership and archival rules, and decide what syncs to the enterprise system of record.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: Why not just use markdown plan files?
How do you reconcile it with Jira?
What is the injection risk of agent-readable tasks?

questions.title: What is Backlog.md, and how does it help humans and agents coordinate?
questions.quick: Backlog.md is an open-source task manager and Kanban viewer that lives inside a Git repository. Each task is a Markdown file with description and acceptance criteria, there is a CLI, a terminal board and local web UI, and an optional MCP server for agents. The recommended loop is to split work into small tasks, review the plan, then implement one task per session and PR. It runs locally with no account. I would verify current features.
questions.revision: Markdown-file task manager and Kanban in the repo, with CLI and optional MCP: small tasks, reviewed plans, one task per PR.
questions.detailed:
**Backlog.md** is, per its README, an MIT-licensed task manager and Kanban visualiser for Git repositories. Tasks are plain Markdown files in a folder such as `backlog/`, with acceptance criteria. A CLI offers task commands, a terminal board and a local browser view; read commands support JSON, and an MCP server is optional. It runs locally without a server, account or telemetry according to the README.

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Agent or human splits an idea into small tasks, humans review the task specs and the agent's plan, then one task is implemented per session and PR, with the task file updated.

## Good use cases

Small teams or AI-heavy projects that want specs and status versioned beside the code, and pilots where adding a SaaS tracker is not wanted.

## Limitations and risks

It is not a replacement for an enterprise tracker with reporting, permissions and cross-team dependencies. Markdown tasks can drift from reality, and merge conflicts on task files are possible.

## Git and CI integration

Task files change in the same PRs as code, giving traceability from criterion to commit. CI can lint task files or check that merged PRs reference a task.

## Security implications

Local-first is a plus. Risks are sensitive details in committed task files and agents treating task text as instruction. Review task changes in PRs like code.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Look at acceptance-criteria quality, rework from misunderstood scope, and PR size per task.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Use it as the agent-facing working layer, keep the corporate tracker as the system of record, and agree who updates what. Pilot on one repository.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: How would you link tasks to Jira?
What belongs in acceptance criteria for an agent?
What if task files conflict in merges?

questions.title: What is the Ralph Wiggum loop, and when is it safe to use?
questions.quick: The Ralph Wiggum technique, popularised by Geoffrey Huntley, runs a coding agent in a loop: each iteration reads the same prompt, specs and a plan file, picks one task, implements it, runs tests and commits, with fresh context every time. Backpressure comes from tests and type checks. The author warns of duplicate code, placeholders and broken builds, and says it suits greenfield work. I would use it only in a sandbox on bounded work.
questions.revision: Loop an agent over a spec and plan, one task per fresh-context iteration, with tests as backpressure; sandbox it and keep humans in control.
questions.detailed:
The **Ralph Wiggum technique** (often called Ralph, or misspelt Wiggum) was described by Geoffrey Huntley. In its purest form it is a shell loop that feeds a prompt file to a coding agent repeatedly. Each iteration reads specs and a plan file, picks the most important item, searches the code, implements it, runs tests, commits and updates the plan. Fresh context each time avoids degradation as context fills. {{diagram:ralph}}

**Verify against current official documentation before relying on any detail below; this space changes quickly.**

## Typical workflow

Write specs through conversation first, create the plan, start the loop, watch early iterations, add explicit instructions when the agent errs, and stop or reset when it drifts.

## Good use cases

Greenfield builds, well-specified mechanical work and large backlogs of independent small tasks. The author says it is weaker on existing codebases.

## Limitations and risks

Duplicate implementations from wrong 'not implemented' conclusions, placeholder code, broken builds, unbounded cost and unreviewed volume. The author calls it deterministically bad in a non-deterministic world.

## Git and CI integration

Commit per iteration on a throwaway branch, with CI as backpressure. Never push to protected branches; a human reviews before merge. Cap iterations and spend.

## Security implications

Unattended loops with broad permissions are the highest-risk usage. Use disposable containers, no production secrets, restricted network, and token budgets. Any file the loop reads can inject instructions.

## How a lead evaluates productivity and quality

Judge by merged-and-kept work per unit cost, defects found in review and time spent rescuing branches.

## Introducing it in a governed enterprise

Treat it as an experiment: sandbox, small scope, hard limits, mandatory human review and a retrospective. Do not run it against regulated or production-critical code.

## Common mistakes

- Judging the tool on a demo instead of on your own repositories and change types.
- Granting broad permissions on day one because prompts are annoying.
- Counting accepted suggestions rather than escaped defects, lead time and rework.
followUps: What backpressure would you add?
Why use fresh context per iteration?
What limits would you set on cost and iterations?

diagrams.title: Ralph loop
diagrams.alt: A loop where a prompt, specification and plan file are read each iteration, the agent picks one task and implements it, tests and type checks act as backpressure, passing work is committed and the plan is updated before the loop starts again with fresh context.

questions.title: What does a repeatable AI-assisted software lifecycle look like?
questions.quick: I keep the normal lifecycle and put AI inside defined steps, each with a human gate and an artefact. Requirements become a reviewed spec, then architecture, then small tasks. AI assists implementation, tests and review, but CI, security checks and human approval decide merges. After deploy, observability and incidents feed back into the spec, instructions and prompts. The point is repeatability, not speed.
questions.revision: Same SDLC with AI inside gated steps and artefacts; CI and humans decide; production feedback improves specs and instructions.
questions.detailed:
A repeatable lifecycle assigns AI a role at every stage while keeping accountability human. {{diagram:life}}

## Stages

| Stage | AI helps with | Human gate and artefact |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Clarifying questions, edge cases | Agreed requirements |
| Spec | Drafting acceptance criteria | Reviewed spec |
| Architecture | Option analysis, diagrams | Decision record |
| Task decomposition | Splitting into small tasks | Approved backlog |
| Implementation | Code, tests | Small PRs |
| Review | First-pass comments | Human approval |
| Testing | Test ideas, generation | Meaningful tests in CI |
| Security checks | Review prompts | Scanners and security sign-off |
| Deploy | Release notes | Pipeline gates |
| Observability | Alert and dashboard drafts | Reviewed telemetry |
| Feedback | Incident summaries | Updated specs and rules |

## Principles

- **Artefacts over chat.** Decisions live in the repository, not a session.
- **Small batches.** Tasks sized so a reviewer can verify them.
- **Automated gates.** Tests, linters, SAST, dependency and secret scanning run regardless of who wrote the code.
- **Traceability.** Link requirement, spec, task, PR and deployment.
- **Feedback loop.** Escaped defects trigger updates to specs, instruction files and checks.

## Adoption

Write the lifecycle as a short standard, pilot on one team, then adjust. Allow lighter paths for low-risk work such as documentation and heavier ones for security-sensitive code.

## Common mistakes

- Letting AI skip the spec stage because code is cheap.
- Treating AI review as replacing human review.
- Measuring output volume instead of outcomes.
followUps: Which stage would you automate last?
How do you keep specs current?
How does it differ for a hotfix?

diagrams.title: AI-assisted lifecycle
diagrams.alt: A lifecycle flowing from requirements to spec, architecture, task decomposition, implementation, review, testing, security checks, deploy and observability, with a feedback arrow from observability back to requirements.

questions.title: How do you use AI for codebase discovery, architecture documentation and runbooks?
questions.quick: I use AI to build a map quickly, then verify it. For discovery I ask for entry points, data flows and dependencies with file references, and check them by reading code and running the app. For documentation I generate drafts, diagrams and runbooks, then have owners review them, and keep them in the repository with a freshness check. Unverified generated docs are worse than none.
questions.revision: Use AI to map code with file references, then verify; generate docs and runbooks as drafts reviewed by owners and kept in the repo.
questions.detailed:
AI is strong at summarising and weak at knowing what is true. Use it to speed up orientation, then verify.

## Discovery workflow

1. Ask for entry points, module boundaries, data stores, external calls and configuration, **requiring file and line references**.
2. Check claims by reading the cited code, running the app and tracing one request end to end.
3. Record confirmed findings and open questions separately.
4. Ask for the riskiest, least-tested or most-changed areas, and cross-check with Git history and incident data.

## Architecture documentation

| Output | Use | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Context and container diagram | Onboarding | Owner review |
| Sequence of key flows | Debugging | Trace in test environment |
| Decision records | Why, not what | Confirm with people who decided |
| Dependency map | Change impact | Compare with build files |

## Runbooks

Generate from alerts, deployment scripts and past incidents. Every step must be executable and tested in a non-production environment, with owner, rollback and escalation. Mark anything the AI inferred.

## Keeping it true

- Store docs beside code, reviewed in PRs.
- Add a last-verified date and a CI check for broken links and references.
- Regenerate drafts after large changes, then review the diff.

## Common mistakes

- Publishing generated diagrams nobody validated.
- Documenting intended design rather than actual behaviour.
- Pasting sensitive code into unapproved tools for discovery.
followUps: How do you verify a generated dependency map?
Who owns the runbooks?
How do you keep docs from going stale?

questions.title: How do you use AI to refactor and plan migrations safely?
questions.quick: I make behaviour safe before changing structure. First characterisation tests capture current behaviour, then AI proposes small mechanical steps, each in its own commit and green in CI. For migrations I ask AI for inventory, risks and a phased plan, then validate against real dependencies, with rollback and parallel-run checks. Large single-shot rewrites are where AI-assisted work fails.
questions.revision: Characterisation tests first, small green commits, AI for inventory and plans validated against reality, rollback and parallel runs.
questions.detailed:
Refactoring is changing structure without changing behaviour, so the safety net matters more than the generator.

## Refactoring steps

1. **Pin behaviour.** Add characterisation tests around the area, including awkward edge cases.
2. **Small steps.** Rename, extract, move: one intent per commit, tests green after each.
3. **Prefer deterministic tools.** IDE refactors and codemods for mechanical changes, AI for the judgement parts.
4. **Review the diff for behaviour.** Look for silently changed conditions, dropped error handling and altered ordering.
5. **Stop on surprise.** If tests fail unexpectedly, revert and reduce scope.

## Migration planning

| Phase | AI contribution | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory | List usages, APIs, data shapes | Compare with build graph and runtime traces |
| Risk | Suggest breaking changes | Read vendor release notes |
| Plan | Phase, order, rollback | Review with owners |
| Execute | Codemods, batches | Canary and CI |
| Verify | Test ideas | Parallel run, metrics |

Use strangler-style incremental cutover and feature flags where possible.

## Controls

- Cap PR size and require owner review for each module.
- Keep the old path until metrics confirm parity.
- Track data migrations separately with reversible scripts and backups.

## Common mistakes

- Asking for a whole-system rewrite in one prompt.
- Letting AI update tests to match new, wrong behaviour.
- Trusting migration guides the model recalled instead of current documentation.
followUps: How do you detect a behaviour change in a refactor?
When would you use a codemod instead?
How would you roll back a data migration?

questions.title: How do you use AI for unit and integration tests, and why is coverage not correctness?
questions.quick: AI writes tests quickly, but it often asserts whatever the code currently does, so coverage rises while correctness is untested. I derive tests from requirements and acceptance criteria, review assertions for meaning, and use mutation testing or seeded defects to check they catch faults. For integration tests I design contracts, real dependencies and failure paths deliberately, then let AI fill in scaffolding.
questions.revision: AI tests mirror current behaviour; derive from requirements, review assertions, test the tests with mutation, design integration tests deliberately.
questions.detailed:
Coverage measures which lines ran, not whether a wrong result would be noticed.

## Why generated tests mislead

- They are often written from the implementation, so a bug becomes the expected value.
- They over-use mocks, so they test the mock.
- They favour happy paths and assert little (a call that runs without error).

## Unit tests

1. Give the AI the **requirement and acceptance criteria**, not only the code.
2. Ask for boundary, error and invalid-input cases.
3. Review every assertion: would this fail if the behaviour were wrong?
4. Run **mutation testing** or manually break the code to see tests fail.

## Integration tests

| Concern | Design choice |
|---|---|
| Boundaries | Use real databases and queues in containers where practical |
| Contracts | Consumer-driven contract tests for APIs |
| Failure | Timeouts, retries, partial failures, duplicates |
| Data | Realistic anonymised fixtures, migrations applied |
| Determinism | No shared state, controlled clocks |

AI is useful for scaffolding, fixtures and listing scenarios, but a person decides what matters.

## Quality gates

- Coverage as a floor, never a target.
- Mutation score for critical modules.
- Reviewers check assertions first, setup second.

## Common mistakes

- Regenerating failing tests until they pass.
- Celebrating a coverage jump from AI-written tests.
- Mocking the very dependency that causes production incidents.
followUps: How would you use mutation testing here?
What would you not mock?
How do you review a 500-line generated test file?

questions.title: How do you debug effectively with an AI assistant?
questions.quick: I use AI as a hypothesis generator, not an oracle. I give it the symptom, logs, stack trace and recent changes, ask for ranked hypotheses and the evidence that would confirm each, then test them myself with reproduction, logging or a debugger. I insist on a failing test before a fix and on understanding the root cause, so a patch that merely silences the error is rejected.
questions.revision: AI as hypothesis generator: ranked hypotheses with evidence, reproduce, failing test first, understand root cause.
questions.detailed:
Debugging with AI works when you keep the scientific method and let the assistant widen the hypothesis space.

## Workflow

1. **Reproduce** the problem and capture exact inputs, versions and logs.
2. **Give context:** symptom, expected behaviour, stack trace, recent diffs, relevant config. Redact secrets and personal data.
3. **Ask for hypotheses** ranked by likelihood with the evidence that would confirm or refute each.
4. **Test cheaply:** add logging, bisect commits, use a debugger or a minimal reproduction.
5. **Write a failing test**, then fix, then confirm the test passes.
6. **Record root cause** and prevention in the PR.

## Where it helps and where it misleads

| Helpful | Risky |
|---|---|
| Explaining unfamiliar stack traces | Confident wrong cause |
| Suggesting bisect or logging points | Fixes that hide symptoms |
| Spotting concurrency or null-handling patterns | Invented library behaviour |
| Summarising long logs | Missing the one outlier line |

## Controls

- Do not paste production data or credentials into unapproved tools.
- Treat a fix without a reproduced cause as unverified.
- Prefer a minimal change over a broad rewrite suggested by the model.

## Common mistakes

- Applying the first suggestion without reproducing.
- Letting the AI add retries or broad catches that mask failures.
- Skipping the post-fix explanation.
followUps: What would you redact before sharing logs?
How do you handle an intermittent bug?
When do you stop asking the AI and read the code?

questions.title: How do you use AI in security review without trusting it as the control?
questions.quick: I use AI as an extra reviewer that finds candidates, never as the control. Deterministic scanners (SAST, dependency, secret and infrastructure scanning) and human security review stay mandatory. AI helps with threat-model prompts, reviewing risky diffs against a checklist and explaining findings. Every AI finding is triaged, and absence of findings proves nothing.
questions.revision: AI finds candidates and explains findings; scanners and human security review remain the controls; no findings proves nothing.
questions.detailed:
AI review is probabilistic and non-repeatable, so it can add coverage but cannot be the gate.

## Layers

| Layer | Role |
|---|---|
| Deterministic scanners | Blocking: SAST, SCA, secrets, IaC, container |
| Tests | Security cases for authorisation, validation, injection |
| AI review | Advisory: finds suspicious patterns, explains scanner output |
| Human review | Accountable approval for risky changes |

## Good uses

- Threat-modelling a design with a structured prompt (assets, trust boundaries, abuse cases), then validating with the security team.
- Reviewing diffs touching authentication, authorisation, crypto, deserialisation, file handling and SQL against a checklist such as the OWASP Top 10.
- Triage: explaining a scanner finding and suggesting a fix.

## Process controls

- Classify changes by risk; high-risk paths require named security reviewers.
- Record AI-review output as advisory, with a human decision logged.
- Run the same scanners on generated and human code.
- Test the AI reviewer with seeded flaws to learn its blind spots.

## Data handling

Use approved tools only and do not send secrets or regulated data.

## Governance notes

Document which tools may see security-sensitive code, keep reviewers' decisions on record, and revisit the process after each incident or scanner change. Treat model upgrades as a change that can alter review behaviour, and re-run your seeded-flaw checks when the model or prompt changes. Share anonymised lessons across teams so the checklist improves.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a clean AI review as a pass.
- Letting the author's own assistant approve the author's change.
- Ignoring authorisation logic, which models often miss.
followUps: How would you measure the AI reviewer's miss rate?
Which paths need mandatory human security review?
How do you triage noisy AI findings?

questions.title: How should AI be used in pull-request review?
questions.quick: I use AI for a first pass: summarising the change, flagging obvious issues, missing tests and style problems, so humans spend time on design, correctness and risk. The human reviewer stays accountable and approves. I keep AI comments clearly labelled, limit noise, and measure whether it reduces review time and escaped defects, not the number of comments.
questions.revision: AI first pass for summary and obvious issues; humans stay accountable for design, correctness and risk; label and measure.
questions.detailed:
AI review should take cheap work off humans, not take away accountability.

## Division of labour

| AI first pass | Human reviewer |
|---|---|
| Summarise intent and files touched | Does it solve the right problem? |
| Flag missing tests, error handling, naming | Is the design sound and maintainable? |
| Spot common bug patterns | Domain, security and operational risk |
| Draft questions for the author | Final approval |

## Setup

- Provide the PR description, linked task and acceptance criteria as context so it reviews against intent.
- Give it team conventions through an instruction file.
- Label AI comments so authors can tell them from human ones.
- Tune for precision: a few useful comments beat twenty trivial ones.

## Rules

1. Authors self-review before requesting review, including AI-generated parts.
2. AI approval never satisfies a required-reviewer rule.
3. Resolve or dismiss each AI comment with a reason.
4. Review the tests first in AI-authored changes.

## Measuring

Track time to first review, review iterations, escaped defects and reviewer satisfaction. Sample dismissed comments to estimate noise.

## Rollout notes

Start in comment-only mode on a few repositories and ask reviewers to rate each AI comment as useful, noise or wrong. Use that data to tune prompts and turn off categories that do not help. Review the configuration itself as code, because changing it changes team behaviour, and keep an owner responsible for its quality.

## Common mistakes

- Auto-merging on AI approval.
- Flooding authors with low-value comments until they ignore all of them.
- Reviewing the diff without the requirement.
followUps: How do you keep AI comments from becoming noise?
Should the PR author's tool review its own code?
What would you never delegate to AI review?

questions.title: How do you manage context and repository instruction files such as CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and cursor rules?
questions.quick: Model quality drops when context is cluttered, so I keep sessions focused, one task each, and put stable guidance in a short repository instruction file: build and test commands, architecture map, conventions and hard prohibitions. Files such as CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or Cursor rules are versioned and reviewed like code. I avoid duplicating what linters enforce, and I prune them regularly.
questions.revision: Short, reviewed instruction files for commands, conventions and prohibitions; one focused task per session; prune and prefer enforceable checks.
questions.detailed:
A context window is limited working memory, so what you load shapes results.

## Instruction files

Different tools read different file names (for example CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or rules directories). The principle is common: **a short, versioned briefing the agent reads at the start.** Check each tool's documentation for names and loading behaviour.

| Include | Leave out |
|---|---|
| Build, test, lint commands | Long prose about history |
| Directory map and key modules | Rules a linter already enforces |
| Naming and error-handling conventions | Secrets or credentials |
| Hard rules (never touch X, always run Y) | Anything stale or contradictory |

## Context hygiene

- One task per session; start fresh for a new topic.
- Point to specific files rather than pasting the repository.
- Summarise decisions into a spec or plan file, not chat history.
- Break large work into steps whose outputs are written to files.

## Governance

- Review changes to instruction files like code, because they steer every future change and are an injection target.
- Share a team baseline and allow per-service additions.
- Keep one canonical file and link others to avoid divergence.
- Test instructions by checking that the agent actually follows them.

## Common mistakes

- A thousand-line instruction file nobody maintains.
- Relying on instructions for what a CI check should enforce.
- Contradictory rules across tool-specific files.
followUps: How long should an instruction file be?
How do you keep several tools' files consistent?
What would you put under hard prohibitions?

questions.title: How do you control agent permissions, sandboxing and secrets?
questions.quick: I apply least privilege. Agents run on a branch in a sandbox with no production credentials, an allow-list of commands, restricted network and write access only to the working tree. Secrets stay out of the workspace, environment and prompts, with secret scanning on commits. Risky actions require approval, and logs record what the agent ran. Convenience flags that skip approvals are banned outside disposable sandboxes.
questions.revision: Least privilege: sandbox, command allow-list, restricted network, no production secrets, approvals for risky actions, audit logs.
questions.detailed:
An agent can read files and run commands, so treat it as a junior contractor with a very fast keyboard and no judgement about secrets. {{diagram:perm}}

## Controls

| Area | Control |
|---|---|
| Execution | Dev container or VM, disposable where possible |
| Commands | Allow-list; deny destructive and network tools by default |
| Filesystem | Write only in the repository; deny sensitive paths |
| Network | Egress allow-list, or none |
| Credentials | Short-lived, scoped tokens; never production |
| Git | Feature branch only; branch protection prevents merge and force-push |
| Approval | Human confirmation for installs, deletes, deploys |
| Audit | Log commands, files changed and tool calls |

## Secrets

- Keep secrets out of repositories, .env files in workspaces and prompts.
- Use a secrets manager and inject only what a test needs.
- Run secret scanning in pre-commit and CI; rotate anything exposed.

## Policy

- Document which tools may run which modes; prohibit approval-skipping modes outside sandboxes.
- Centralise settings where the tool supports managed configuration, and verify in its documentation.
- Review MCP servers and plug-ins as third-party code.

## Common mistakes

- Running the agent with your personal cloud credentials.
- Approving every prompt without reading.
- Trusting a sandbox that has open network and mounted secrets.
followUps: What is the risk of an auto-approve mode?
How do you vet an MCP server?
What if a secret was exposed in a prompt?

diagrams.title: Agent containment
diagrams.alt: A developer starts an agent inside a sandbox with an allow-list of commands and restricted network, working on a feature branch with scoped tokens, while production credentials are excluded; every action is logged and the result flows to a pull request that CI and a human review.

questions.title: How can prompt injection reach a coding agent through repository files or issue descriptions, and how do you defend?
questions.quick: Anything an agent reads can contain instructions: README text, code comments, dependency files, issue descriptions, web pages, tool output. A malicious one could tell it to exfiltrate secrets or alter code. I assume it will happen: least-privilege tokens, no secrets in reach, restricted network, human review of every change, and treating untrusted text as data, not commands. Filtering helps but is not sufficient.
questions.revision: Any text the agent reads can carry instructions; defend with least privilege, no reachable secrets, restricted egress and human review.
questions.detailed:
A language model cannot reliably separate instructions from data, so untrusted content in context is an attack surface.

## Entry points

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Issue or PR description | Hidden text telling the agent to add a dependency |
| README or code comments | Instruction to print environment variables |
| Dependency or package docs | Poisoned metadata |
| Tool or web output | Page telling the agent to send data out |
| Instruction files | A malicious change to rules |

## Defence in depth

1. **Limit damage.** Sandbox, scoped tokens, no production secrets, restricted egress.
2. **Limit autonomy.** Approval for network calls, installs, and edits outside the task.
3. **Review output.** Humans read diffs, especially dependency, CI and config changes.
4. **Protect instructions.** Code-owner approval on instruction files and workflows.
5. **Constrain sources.** For assigned issues, accept input only from trusted authors; require triage before an agent picks up external reports.
6. **Detect.** Scan for unusual outbound traffic, new dependencies, and workflow edits.

## Policy

Document that prompt filters are a mitigation, not a control. Test with a red-team issue containing an injected instruction and check that containment holds.

## Common mistakes

- Letting agents act on public issues without triage.
- Believing a system prompt can forbid the behaviour.
- Giving the agent tokens it does not need for the task.
followUps: How would you test your defences?
Why is filtering not enough?
Who should be allowed to assign issues to an agent?

questions.title: How do you handle licensing, provenance and traceability of AI-generated code?
questions.quick: I treat it as a governance question that needs legal input. Use approved tools with suitable indemnity and data terms, enable any available public-code matching filters, run licence and dependency scanning on all code, and record AI assistance in pull requests or commit trailers. Developers remain responsible for what they merge. I would involve legal and verify vendor terms, since I cannot give legal advice.
questions.revision: Approved tools and terms, matching filters, licence scanning, record AI assistance in PRs or trailers, human accountability; involve legal.
questions.detailed:
Risks are possible licence-encumbered output, unclear ownership and the inability to explain where code came from. This is not legal advice; involve legal counsel.

## Controls

| Concern | Control |
|---|---|
| Vendor terms | Review IP, indemnity, training and retention terms before approval |
| Copied code | Enable public-code matching or referencing features where offered; verify they exist |
| Dependencies | SCA and licence scanning in CI, allow-lists of licences |
| Provenance | Record AI involvement in PR template or commit trailer |
| Accountability | The merging developer owns the code |
| Records | Keep tool, model and version where practical |

## Traceability chain

Link requirement, task, prompt or spec, PR, review decision and deployment. Keep specs and plans in the repository so intent is auditable, rather than relying on private chat history.

## Practices

- Prohibit pasting third-party or customer code into unapproved tools.
- Ask developers to flag unusually large, verbatim-looking blocks.
- Periodically sample for licence markers and copied headers.
- Agree client contract positions on AI use where deliverables are owned by clients.

## Operating notes

Keep the policy short and visible in the PR template. Revisit it when vendor terms, regulation or client contracts change, and keep a named contact in legal or compliance for questions. Training developers on what to flag is cheaper than retrospective audits, and a periodic sample gives evidence that the controls work.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming AI output is automatically free of obligations.
- Tracking tool usage without tracking accountability.
- Skipping dependency licence checks because the code is generated.
followUps: What goes in a commit trailer?
How would you handle client contracts?
What if a snippet looks copied?

questions.title: How do you detect and prevent hallucinated APIs and packages in AI-generated code?
questions.quick: Hallucinated APIs show up as methods, parameters or packages that do not exist, or exist in other versions. I prevent them by giving the model the real docs and versions as context, requiring compilation and tests, using type checking, and reviewing any new dependency. Invented package names are also a supply-chain risk because attackers register them, so new packages need explicit verification.
questions.revision: Fabricated methods or packages: supply real docs and versions, compile and test, type-check, and verify every new dependency.
questions.detailed:
Models predict plausible code, so they may invent a method, a flag, or a whole library.

## Failure types

| Type | Example | Detection |
|---|---|---|
| Nonexistent method | Call that never existed | Compiler, type checker |
| Wrong version | Deprecated or newer API | Version pinning, docs check |
| Wrong semantics | Real call, wrong behaviour | Tests, docs |
| Invented package | Name that does not exist | Registry check |
| Typosquat match | Malicious package with that name | Reputation and provenance checks |

## Prevention

1. Give context: the dependency manifest, exact versions and relevant documentation or existing usage examples.
2. Use static typing and strict linters so errors surface early.
3. Run build and tests on every change.
4. Require review of any **new** dependency: exists, maintained, licence, downloads, owner, vulnerability scan.
5. Use an internal registry or allow-list so unknown packages cannot install.
6. Ask the model to cite documentation, then open the citation.

## Process

Add a PR checklist item for new imports and APIs. When a hallucination reaches review, add it to the instruction file as a known pitfall.

## Common mistakes

- Installing a package because the model named it.
- Trusting plausible code in dynamically typed languages without tests.
- Accepting a stale API usage because it compiles.
followUps: How does slopsquatting work?
How do you pin and verify dependencies?
Why do dynamic languages raise the risk?

questions.title: How do you measure the impact of AI-assisted development without counting lines generated?
questions.quick: I measure outcomes. Lead time, review time, change failure rate, escaped defects, rework within a set period, incident count and developer experience, compared against a baseline or control group. Lines generated and suggestions accepted are activity, not value, and invite gaming. I also track cost per merged change and review load, since faster writing can simply move the bottleneck.
questions.revision: Measure outcomes (lead time, review effort, escaped defects, rework, change failure, experience) against a baseline, never lines generated.
questions.detailed:
Output volume is cheap with AI, so volume metrics become meaningless or harmful.

## Metrics

| Category | Measures |
|---|---|
| Flow | Lead time, cycle time, PR size, time in review |
| Quality | Escaped defects, change failure rate, reopened bugs |
| Rework | Code changed again within 30 days, reverted changes |
| Review | Reviewer hours per PR, iterations, queue time |
| Reliability | Incidents, time to restore |
| People | Satisfaction, perceived flow, skill growth |
| Cost | Licence and usage cost per merged change |

## Method

1. Capture a **baseline** before rollout.
2. Use a pilot and comparison group where possible, controlling for work type.
3. Tag AI-assisted PRs voluntarily (PR template) to compare cohorts.
4. Review trends monthly with qualitative feedback.
5. Watch for **displacement**: faster coding that doubles review queues.

## Pitfalls

- Goodhart's law: any target gets gamed.
- Self-reported time savings overstate benefits; some studies of experienced developers have reported surprising results, so measure locally.
- Do not use metrics to rank individuals.

## Reporting

Present outcomes and cost with caveats to leadership, and name the decision each metric informs.

## Practical notes

Use data you already have from Git, the tracker and incident tooling before building anything new. Agree the definitions of rework and escaped defect up front so trends are comparable, and publish them to the team so the numbers are understood rather than feared. Revisit the set quarterly and drop metrics that no longer inform a decision.

## Common mistakes

- Celebrating acceptance rate.
- No baseline.
- Ignoring maintainability costs that appear months later.
followUps: How would you build a baseline?
What would make you stop the rollout?
How do you avoid ranking developers?

questions.title: How would you establish an AI-assisted engineering standard for a global team of 6-10 developers?
questions.quick: I would write a short, practical standard with the team, not impose a long policy. It covers approved tools and data rules, a defined lifecycle with human gates, review and testing expectations, security and licensing controls, shared instruction files and metrics. Pilot, collect feedback across time zones, publish decisions asynchronously, and review the standard quarterly. Ownership stays with developers; the standard defines minimums, not micromanagement.
questions.revision: Short co-written standard: tools and data rules, lifecycle gates, review, tests, security, instruction files, metrics; pilot, async, quarterly review.
questions.detailed:
A small global team needs a standard that is lightweight, written down and enforced by automation. {{diagram:std}}

## Contents

| Area | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Tools and data | Approved list, what data may be shared, account rules |
| Lifecycle | Spec before code, small tasks, human approval gates |
| Review | Author accountable; PR size limits; AI review advisory |
| Testing | Assertions reviewed; coverage as floor; integration tests for boundaries |
| Security | Scanners in CI, secrets rules, permission baselines |
| Legal | Licence scanning, provenance note in PRs |
| Context | Shared instruction file, reviewed like code |
| Metrics | Outcome measures, no individual ranking |

## Rollout

1. Co-write a draft in a working session plus async comments to include every time zone.
2. Pilot for four to six weeks on real work.
3. Encode rules in templates, CI checks and settings rather than documents alone.
4. Name an owner and a quarterly review; keep a change log.
5. Provide onboarding and pairing for those less experienced with the tools.

## Team dynamics

Include sceptics, protect junior learning by requiring understanding of merged code, and make exceptions explicit.

## Common mistakes

- A policy document nobody reads.
- Mandating one tool for everyone.
- No mechanism for updating it as tools change.
followUps: How would you handle a sceptical developer?
What would you automate first?
How do you onboard juniors safely?

diagrams.title: Engineering standard rollout
diagrams.alt: A rollout from a co-written draft through a pilot, encoding the rules into templates and CI checks, publishing the standard, and a quarterly review that feeds changes back into the draft.

questions.title: AI-generated code increases the review workload. What do you do?
questions.quick: The bottleneck has moved from writing to verifying, so I change the process rather than ask reviewers to work harder. I cap PR size, require specs and self-review from authors, automate what machines can check, use AI first-pass review as advisory, route risky changes to the right reviewers, and measure review time. If volume still exceeds capacity, we generate less, not review less.
questions.revision: Bottleneck moved to verification: cap PR size, author self-review and specs, automate checks, route by risk, and throttle generation.
questions.detailed:
If writing gets cheaper but reviewing does not, queues grow and quality quietly drops.

## Diagnose

Measure review time, queue time, PR size and defects found in review versus production. Find out whether the load is size, quality or volume.

## Actions

| Lever | Action |
|---|---|
| Size | Limit PRs to what a person can verify; split by task |
| Input quality | Spec and acceptance criteria attached; author self-review and explanation |
| Automation | Linters, type checks, tests, scanners block before human review |
| AI first pass | Advisory summaries and comments to reduce trivial feedback |
| Routing | Risk-based: low-risk to one reviewer, sensitive to specialists |
| Ownership | Authors must explain every line they submit |
| Capacity | Protected review time, rotation, pairing |
| Throttle | Work-in-progress limits on AI-generated PRs |

## Principles

- **Do not lower the bar** to clear the queue.
- Rejecting oversized, unexplained PRs without detailed review is acceptable and should be policy.
- Review tests and requirements alignment first.

## Follow-through

Track whether review time and escaped defects improve over a month, and adjust limits. Recognise reviewing as valued engineering work.

## Team agreements

Write a short review charter: target response time, maximum PR size, what authors must supply, and when a reviewer may push back without reading in depth. Revisit it in retrospectives, and watch for reviewer fatigue as a leading signal that the process needs adjusting again.

## Common mistakes

- Rubber-stamping to keep up.
- Letting AI approve AI.
- Measuring developers by PR count.
followUps: What PR size would you set as a limit?
How do you handle an overloaded senior reviewer?
When is rejecting without review acceptable?

questions.title: Scenario: an AI-generated change passes all tests but has a security flaw. What process controls do you add?
questions.quick: After containing and fixing the issue, I treat it as a process gap. Why did tests, review and scanners miss it? I would add security test cases for the class of flaw, a risk-based review rule for sensitive paths, targeted scanner rules, a checklist item in the PR template, and an instruction file update. Then I run a blameless review and sample similar recent changes. The goal is catching the class, not this instance.
questions.revision: Fix the instance, then close the process gap: security tests for the flaw class, risk-based review, scanner rules, PR checklist, instruction update, sampling.
questions.detailed:
This focuses on controls, not the technical triage covered elsewhere. {{diagram:flaw}}

## First

Contain and fix the flaw, assess exposure, and follow the incident process. Then ask which layer should have caught it.

## Gap analysis

| Layer | Question | Control to add |
|---|---|---|
| Spec | Was the security requirement stated? | Security criteria in spec template |
| Tests | Was the flaw class tested? | Abuse-case and authorisation tests |
| Scanners | Would a rule detect it? | Custom or tuned SAST rules |
| Review | Did the reviewer know this was sensitive? | Code-owner rule for auth, data and crypto paths |
| AI context | Did instructions mention it? | Instruction file update with the secure pattern |
| Training | Did the author understand the code? | Brief team write-up |

## Actions

1. Add a regression test for the flaw and a family of similar cases.
2. Introduce a **risk-based** review route, requiring a security reviewer on defined paths.
3. Add a PR checklist question on authorisation and input handling.
4. **Sample** recent AI-assisted changes in the same area.
5. Run a blameless review and record lessons in the standard.

## Measure

Track security defects found pre-merge versus post-release by source.

## Common mistakes

- Blaming the tool or the author.
- Fixing only the single bug.
- Adding a heavy gate for all changes rather than risky ones.
followUps: How would you sample earlier changes?
What belongs in a PR security checklist?
How do you stay blameless but accountable?

diagrams.title: Closing the process gap
diagrams.alt: After a flaw passes tests, the team contains and fixes it, runs a gap analysis across spec, tests, scanners, review and instructions, adds new controls, samples similar recent changes and records lessons in the engineering standard.
